title: ‘Alley Cats’ Review: Ricky Gervais’ Half-Crass, Half-Sappy, Mostly Unmemorable Netflix Cartoon
full_text: × Skip to main content By Angie Han Plus Icon Angie Han Television Critic ajhan Follow Sign Up View All August 7, 2026 12:01am 'Alley Cats' Netflix It’s been my experience that people who hate cats and people who love them describe them exactly the same way; it’s only the tone that differs. The former scowl as they complain that, “Cats are such jerks.” The latter say it with an indulgent smile. To the feline fan club, of which I count myself as a card-carrying member, a-hole behavior is part of the allure — they’re so stubbornly, fascinatingly, often hilariously self-interested that even the dim bulbs seem possessed of complete inner lives. Besides, they’re not always mean. Just as often, they can make you melt with their softness, their sensitivity, their loyalty. Related Stories TV Ricky Gervais Pitches Animation Debut 'Alley Cats' at Annecy Masterclass: "I Could Make This Forever" Movies Netflix Unveils 'Ray Gunn' First Look, 'Ghostbusters: Night Shift' at Annecy Alley Cats The Bottom Line Short but shaggy. Airdate: Friday, Aug. 7 (Netflix) Cast: Ricky Gervais, Tom basden, Jo Hartley, David Earl, Diane Morgan, Andrew Brooke, Kerry Godliman, Tony Way, Natalie Cassidy Creator: Ricky Gervais Alley Cats , Ricky Gervais ’ new animated series for Netflix, gets that much. In the manner of my own furry sons, the show follows its own unhurried rhythm, turning on a dime between casually vicious and ooey-gooey sweet. But lacking the creative depth to make either tone land, it winds up a comedy of existential angst that’s rarely all that funny and only occasionally kind of moving. In addition to writing and directing, Gervais leads the cast as Gus, a chunky orange fella who’s the de facto leader of a gang of strays. To call them a ragtag bunch would be putting it politely; though the animation by Blink Industries is clean and crisp, the cats’ personalities are anything but. Fang (Andrew Brooke) is a beefy tuxedo perpetually raring for a fight. Olive (Diane Morgan) is an orange space cadet desperate to breed. One mangy beast is simply called Puke (David Earl), presumably for the sort of reaction he tends to elicit with his many tales of screwing and/or eating every disgusting thing you can imagine. The only one of their number fit for polite society is Ponce (Tom Basden), a pet cat whose primary function within the clique is to get dragged for everything from his lack of balls to the way he says the word “interesting.” Every day begins with the crew in the abandoned hovel they call home, watching whatever happens to be airing — dating shows, history docs, news reports — on a TV that somehow still works. Eventually they’ll head outside to look for food, visit friends and foes, settle whatever silly argument has been sparked by their latest viewing (e.g., “Are bees scary?” or “Could four cats murder a human child?”). Then they’ll retire back to their shack, to do it all again tomorrow. Gervais has said that the voice performances were captured in group sessions rather than solo ones, and it shows in the relaxed chemistry of the cast. They sound like nothing so much as a group of longtime pals busting each other’s balls over a third round of beers, and there’s some appeal in getting to sit with that loose and shaggy vibe. But as anyone who’s been seated next to a group of longtime pals busting each other’s balls over a third round of beers knows, just because they find themselves entertaining doesn’t mean it’s inherently interesting to listen to them. Though the season runs just six episodes, each under 20 minutes, it feels much longer when so many of those minutes are spent on aimless, mindless chatter. The cats’ low-key routine is interrupted when, during one of their daily outings, they encounter a tiny gray kitten (Jo Hartley) who’s gotten lost. In a burst of generosity, Gus promises Kitten they’ll help return her home. Their efforts (primarily, wandering around until Kitten spots a home that looks familiar) comprise what amounts to the season’s driving plot — though in typical feline fashion, it’s never long before they’re waylaid by one random side quest or other. Alley Cat functions in two sharply distinct modes. The first is rude, crude shit-talking. Gus, Fang, Puke — and, okay, not so much Ponce — spend their days riffing about the things they’ve done or want to do with their dicks, bickering about who’s tougher than whom, showering each other with elaborate insults. One particularly self-satisfied diatribe ends with Gus imagining Puke dying from AIDS after getting sodomized by infected monkeys; it’s edgy in a way that’s sure to impress tweens whose parents have just removed the controls from their Netflix profiles, and not many others. Mostly, though, their conversations just blend into an undifferentiated drone of meaningless sniping, lurid sexual descriptions, colorful empty threats and many, many bad words. If you think a lengthy exchange about whether “Bitches be trippin'” is a Gandhi quote — Gus insists yes, Ponce correctly disagrees — is the height of hilarity, maybe you’ll find the cats’ chats more amusing then I did. The other tone Alley Cats traffics in is an almost cloying sentimentality. As braggadocious as Gus and his friends can be, they’re acutely aware of both their insignificance and vulnerability. Cats they know are hit by cars, replaced by supposedly loving owners, left to wither away in some dirty corner; as one sadly puts it, they’re all just “future roadkill.” Kitten’s wide-eyed questions about the permanence of death or the cruelty of humans only further underline how painful the mere fact of existence can be. But Kitten’s presence also, naturally, encourages Gus to open up, and show a softer, happier side as he sings to her or cuddles her or generally guides her through life’s terrible uncertainties. In one vulnerable moment, he even tries to bargain with a God he’s not convinced exists — shocking stuff from a character created and performed by one of pop culture’s most exhaustingly noisy atheists. It’s all very moving in theory, and less so in practice. These two-note characters simply aren’t built to shoulder such heavy yet predictable emotionality. But then, I guess, neither are real cats. I might have big existential feelings about my own kitties — the purpose I get from caring for them, the joy I get from loving them, the preemptive grief I experience knowing that they will die in the hopefully very distant but definitely inevitable future. I might thus relate pretty well to Gus’ protectiveness of Kitten, to Kitten’s heartbreak at how indifferent the world can be to animals, to the gang’s sorrow as they watch an aging acquaintance carted off for euthanasia. My cats themselves, though, I suspect would more likely relate to the show’s opening scene. “What was that for?” complains Ponce, after getting a swat to the face. “I’m a cat. That’s just what cats do,” Gus shrugs in return. It’s not a satisfying reply. But it is, indeed, just what cats do. THR

title: Meet Nicolaas Schmidt, the German Filmmaker Who Thinks “Plain Banality Is Stimulating as F***”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 7, 2026 12:01am 'September Afternoon' Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival When the Locarno Film Festival unveiled the program for its 79th edition , it promised an “adventurous” lineup . German filmmaker Nicolaas Schmidt’s debut feature film, September Afternoon , which will world premiere on Aug. 10 in the Filmmakers of the Present Competition of the Swiss festival, is perhaps the perfect case in point. “If you don’t know anything about what’s to come, you are probably at risk of leaving the room,” Locarno’s artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro tells THR . “I’m aware of that, but if you stick with it, you will be completely surprised” and enjoy a cinematic journey you won’t forget any time soon. Related Stories Movies Jean Lodge, British Actress and Mother of 'Nanny' Actor Charles Shaughnessy, Dies at 99 TV The Man Behind David Lynch, Kathryn Bigelow and 'Beverly Hills, 90210' Is Getting His Moment at Locarno What he means is that, just like in Schmidt’s short- and medium-length films, there isn’t much traditional “action” or even dialogue in September Afternoon . “The film uses ‘dead time’ as raw material,” the filmmaker highlights in a director’s note. “I stretch mundane moments until they collapse in their emptiness — an invitation to the viewer. In an age of arbitrary extraordinariness, plain banality is stimulating as fuck.” Schmidt, who was born in Leipzig and lives and works in Hamburg as a filmmaker, video and conceptual artist, tells THR that he is most interested in images, sounds, music and moods, putting a spotlight on the passage of time in everyday situations, repetition and silences. ‘September Afternoon,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Or, as Nazzaro offers: “Maybe the trivialities we see are exactly the things that we might be sorely missing in the future,” says Nazzaro, “because we will not have the time to get bored and tend to trivial matters. So for me, [Schmidt’s work] also brings with it a very political element – how to regain agency over the use of your time.” But wait, what can we share about September Afternoon without spoiling too much? Well, the film shows a couple that refuses to accept that summer is over; instead ​, the small family is ​heading to the coast for ​a​​ last experience with sand and seawater. But they find themselves struggling with strong wind and the encroaching elements. With romantic expectations of the summer flipped on their head, Locarno teases that things unravel from there “into a disaster of a different magnitude,” underlining the filmmaker’s invitation to observe and be surprised. Produced by Maxi Haslberger and Balthasar Busmann, September Afternoon features cinematography by Thomas Oswald. Schmidt directed and edited the movie based on his screenplay. The cast features Amin Motallebzadeh, Katharina Grossmann, Hedi Grossmann and Ada Kurzhöfer. Kino Rebelde is handling international sales. September Afternoon is the second Schmidt film traveling to Locarno. His First Time [The Time for All but Sunset — Violet] premiered at the Swiss festival in 2021 and received a Pardi di Domani special mention. Nicolaas Schmidt Courtesy of Nicolaas Schmidt On his website, the filmmaker describes himself as a “gréyalisateur,” ​emphasizing grey as a midpoint, average – or rather, relativity and ambivalence – ​and the French word for director, “réalisateur,” or someone who brings a film to life. He also calls himself a “dozing artist (concept, photo, video).” And his bio on the website highlights: “He started dreaming at the age of four after visiting the movie theater in his socialist small town south of Leipzig for the very first time” before the GDR and West Germany reunited. Asked about the inspiration for his films, Schmidt tells THR : “It’s all based on ​experiences, ​observations or interpretations of observations.” In the case of September Afternoon , he recalls: “I experienced a similar situation that was as unrelaxed as can be. And I was ​sadly disappointed​ that I didn’t film or didn’t have a friend with a hand camera there to film.” Does he have a detailed plan or script? “I think in detail about what ​exactly ​happens and what is said despite starting the process with wanting to leave things as open as possible,” including for the actors,” he says. “But sometimes things get too ​concrete​ and go beyond what really interests me, and then I pare back.” ‘September Afternoon,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival The process of filming September Afternoon came with some surprises. “When we shot the film, it was late September and really stormy, which made things much harder than expected,” Schmidt explains. “I had originally planned to make the wind seem stronger than it was. ​But my experience so far has shown that it’s good for the films when some things turn out differently than anticipated. While that stresses me out immensely, getting through it together with others does me a world of good and provides me with longer-lasting stability.” Music plays a key role in Schmidt’s films, even though he says he couldn’t compose any himself, and so do commercials. “​In the ’90s, there were commercials that were extremely elaborate and visually captivating, almost poetic, yet emotionally manipulative – that fascinated me, he shares. “I had an interest in them. And I think these are spots people recognize. In the case of September Afternoon , the commercial came late in the process. It is an element that adds ambiguity.” Schmidt has also referenced other movies in his films, with his latest including a scene from Philippe Garrel’s Le Révélateur . How do these cinematic “quotes” find their way into his works? “I find these in the very long development processes,” he tells THR . “I bring together a bigger collection of ideas, thoughts and associations, saved in a wide chaotic note, and bring them into question and a rating and priority structure at some later point, at the latest when I name that work. When a feeling for the film arises then, it’s also less sober and dry than it sounds now.” ‘September Afternoon,’ courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival ​​Late in September Afternoon , there is a scene using light in a specific way, and Schmidt made sure not to simply copy ​the very specific solutions of ​other directors​ “for no reason​​​.” He highlights: “I don’t want to repeat ​every​​​thing.” ​The effect used in the end was “common enough and, in all its simplicity, also effective enough,” the filmmaker explains. Some may say not much happens over long passages of Schmidt’s films, but the creative doesn’t believe that movies need “action.” “That’s not my thing at all. That provokes me to the max,” he tells THR . “But it is a core problem that you must convince people that ​less, or ​nothing, happening can be​ okay or even ​​ ​fascinating and also that you don’t need dialogue.” The same goes for uniform tastes and approaches. “I find it hard to handle uniformity,” Schmidt says. “It ​​unsettles​​ and ​frightens​ me if people subject themselves to ​trends, fashions and ​the whims of the masses,​ or individuals​. I understand that this view also excludes things, but I ​just don’t like any adaptation without questioning and a valid reason.” That said, he doesn’t make films simply to provoke audiences, but out of curiosity and also to potentially discover a community of people outside the mainstream. “​For me, it’s a pretty reliable opportunity to find like-minded people,” Schmidt says. “And I appreciate it when people come up to me and give me the feeling that I am a bit normal.” THR

title: Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review
full_text: Aug 7, 2026 12:01am PT Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review By Alison Herman Plus Icon Alison Herman TV Critic aherman2006 Latest Ricky Gervais’ Netflix Animated Comedy ‘Alley Cats’ Is Surprisingly Bittersweet: TV Review 3 hours ago FX’s Adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ ‘The Shards’ Can’t Be Saved by a Strong Lead Performance: TV Review 2 days ago ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Is Both a Promising Reboot and a Tedious Sequel: TV Review 2 days ago See All Courtesy of Netflix To kick off the third episode of the Netflix animated comedy “ Alley Cats ,” protagonist Gus — an overweight orange tabby voiced by writer, creator and frequent director Ricky Gervais (think Garfield with a distinctly working class British accent) — describes his plan for the day. It starts with an achievable goal. Then: “Get distracted immediately. Do loads of weird, pointless shit that somehow makes stuff worse. Kill something. Eat bits of it. Give up our mission. Come home here. Sleep for 14 hours.” Related Stories Locarno’s Match Me! Projects Push New Voices, Timely Relevance and Authenticity as a Younger Generation Moves Center Stage Gareth Edwards Exits 'Jurassic World Rebirth' Sequel Over Creative Differences “Home,” in this case, is a derelict London rowhouse where Gus and his mates Puke (David Earl), Fang (Andrew Brooke) and Olive (Diane Morgan, better known as daft presenter Philomena Cunk ) have taken to squatting. There, the cats watch TV, from a “Love Island” knockoff called “Thick and Single” to news footage of looting to nature documentaries, chat about nothing and generally do as Gus describes. “Alley Cats” ambles along as such for half a dozen sub-20-minute chapters — though the show is tinged throughout with a melancholy that’s a little surprising from the typically acerbic Gervais. Popular on Variety Given the other series’ swift cancellation , it’s unlikely many viewers will have watched both “Alley Cats” and “Kevin,” the Amazon Prime Video series with a similar premise co-created by Aubrey Plaza. But comparing the two, as is inevitable for a critic commissioned to review each in turn, proves instructive. Both are cartoons for adults distributed via streaming, centered on feline protagonists in major cities. Yet “Kevin” is louder, wackier and more joke-dense — one might even say more American — than “Alley Cats,” which is more downbeat and droll by comparison. “Alley Cats” also organizes itself around social caste, as befits its country of origin. The titular crew also hang around with a housecat they nickname Ponce (Tom Basden), who’s more genteel in every sense of the term than his friends. He sounds posh; he’s spoiled with pudding; he’s neutered and thus immune to baser urges, including Olive’s unrequited crush. The rest of the crew are more base, volleying the c-word — rhymes with “runt” — around freely as they debate useless topics like whether four cats could take down “one fat kid” or if bees are edible. (Most laughs come from these mumbled, mundane exchanges rather than conventional setups and punchlines.) Puke, the mangiest of the group, admits his private parts are “smashed up” because “I gave a hedgehog anal.” But “Alley Cats” doesn’t just revel in the nastiness of feral life. The show also depicts its hardships with disarming frankness, even verging on despondency. An associate of the crew is introduced and then fatally run over in seconds. A deadbeat dad is reassured that, since his kittens were adopted and grew into well-adjusted triplets, “maybe you not being around was their best chance.” The last line of the season — not really a spoiler, since there’s not much context necessary — is “we’re all gonna die soon.” Sometimes, this undercurrent of gloom tips over into outright nihilism. (“Fuck people,” Gus proclaims in one of his many rants at the television. “I can’t wait for people to wipe people off the face of the Earth.”) More often, though, the mood is more one of resignation to a hardscrabble existence that also has its pleasures. The serialized plot of “Alley Cats” comes from a lost kitten (Jo Hartley) the strays resolve to help find her way back home. Gervais isn’t overtly sentimental in depicting Gus’ growing affection for his young, quite cutely drawn (her eyes are enormous) young charge; in fact, the story resolves on a fittingly bittersweet note for the overall tone. But there is a real tenderness that’s thrown into the mix with the lewd banter and glass-half-empty outlook. “Alley Cats” is so compressed that it ends up stopping short of real heft. A subplot about Gus’ ailing mother is introduced so hastily it almost bewilders; on a broader level, this is fundamentally a hangout sitcom about free-range felines. The show nonetheless takes an unexpected direction that makes for an enjoyably low-key binge. Even bullshitting cats have feelings. All six episodes of “Alley Cats” are now streaming on Netflix. title: ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller
full_text: Aug 6, 2026 11:59pm PT ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller Your pandemic lockdown memories have nothing on the end-of-days scenario outlined in this Netflix offering from director Louis Leterrier, which gets by on clammy atmosphere even if it makes no real sense. By Guy Lodge Plus Icon Guy Lodge Film Critic @guylodge Latest ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller 2 hours ago ‘Super Troopers 3’ Review: A Cult Comedy Franchise Seeks No Converts in Instantly Forgettable Third Go-Round 2 days ago ‘One Night Only’ Review: Monica Barbaro and Callum Turner Are Too Hot for This Sexless Sex Comedy 2 days ago See All ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection A decade or so ago, the premise of apocalyptic thriller “ The Last House ” might have sounded a little more out there than it does now: A middle-class Seattle family wakes up one morning to find themselves sealed inside their house with no means of escape, a mysterious enforced house arrest that turns out to be indefinite. Post-Covid, of course, this instead plays as a fantastical spin on an experience still fresh in everyone’s minds — a familiarity that Louis Leterrier ‘s film, all too aptly premiering on Netflix , uses to its claustrophobic advantage. The lockdown imposed on these four people and their immediate neighbors — and who knows how many others — may be of a more extreme and uncanny variety than the mandate that kept most of us home in 2020, but this high-concept chamber piece returns viewers to that mindset of protective panic and uncertainty. Related Stories Cannes' Critics' Week Reveals Lineup of Armenian Filmmakers Taking Part in Next Step Studio Program (EXCLUSIVE) Cannes Critics’ Week Film 'Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building' Sells to Strand Releasing for North America (EXCLUSIVE) The hows and whys of “The Last House” take it into science-fiction territory — lightly and allusively so at first, but eventually with more concrete, effects-heavy world-building (and unbuilding). But the film is most compelling throughout as a straightforward domestic drama, with increasingly fraught family dynamics lending proceedings a baseline of credibility even as whatever’s happening outside the house remains largely inscrutable. Grounded, empathetic performances by Wagner Moura and Greta Lee , as parents hanging onto their adult authority by a thread, deserve much of the credit for that, as does the intricately detailed, changeable design and conception of the house that, in a short time, becomes the characters’ entire world. Popular on Variety “The Last House” mostly works as a tensely enjoyable ride for times of environmental anxiety, though whether there’s any substantial meaning or resonance to the what-if scenario devised by screenwriter Matthew Robinson (“Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die”) is open to question. The film touches on ideas of climate change and ecosystemic adaptation, as well as to both the virtues and limitations of community spirit, but they’re not very deeply or provocatively probed — settling for loose platitudes doled out by an unidentified female narrator. “We lived closer to each other then,” she says at the outset, describing the world before the great shut-in. “But it was easy to feel alone.” Not that there’s much room for loneliness in the close-knit Delgado family, who are introduced making early Christmas plans as winter sets in: They live comfortably, even if engineer dad Jason (Moura) is currently out of work, and happily, even if pre-teen siblings Graham (Noah Alexander Sosnowski) and Ruth (Riley Chung) squabble on the regular. Mom Ann (Lee) frets about signs of structural damage in their roomy midcentury home, but overall, they have it better than most — especially when, with a heavy November rainstorm raging outside, they find they literally can’t leave the house. Doors and windows are rendered unopenable by some outside force; attempts to break the glass prove likewise futile. Others in their street, they discover, are similarly trapped; with the internet down and phone signals cut, they can only guess at how widespread the crisis is. At least early on, a spirit of plucky resilience prevails: Neighbors communicate by signboards, food is lightly rationed, and family movie nights alternate the only two DVDs in the house. (“Annie” and “Air Force One,” hilariously.) But as days turn to weeks, and a spartan Christmas gives way to a very unhappy new year, the family must consider the possibility that this is a grim new normal. If Robinson’s script is fuzzy on the logistics of who or what is keeping them inside — the explanation, when it does arrive, doesn’t exactly hold water, though Leterrier builds up to the reveal with eerie flashes of life outside the living-room window — it’s stronger on the tensions playing out indoors. As the situation grows increasingly dire, Jason and Ann are caught between their gentler duties as parents and more harshly pragmatic survival instincts; Graham and Ruth, both characters drawn, cast and played with unusual nuance, must grow up fast without any wider society to show them the way. Notwithstanding the absurdly particular conditions of its drama, “The Last House” should resonate with anyone attempting to raise children in a world physically changing before our eyes — if it raises some glum existential questions, at least Jason’s ingenious MacGyver-style apocalypse hacks offer comparative light relief. A French genre journeyman whose credits range from “The Incredible Hulk” to “Fast X,” Leterrier keeps it all ticking with the requisite balance of itchy cabin-fever atmospherics and more expansive action setpieces — though given its sometimes chintzy digital effects, the film is most effective when it plays on what you cannot see. Kevin Jenkins’ production design is the most consistent technical asset here, attentive to the detailed wear and tear of the Delgados’ moldering house as it literally cracks under pressure, as well as the ways in which it’s modified to protect and sustain its inhabitants. But there’s still everyday mess and clutter in evidence, at every stage of its evolution: “The Last House” may be silly in some respects, but it has a stabilizing sense of how life actually goes on when everything ends. ‘The Last House’ Review: Wagner Moura and Greta Lee Bring Conviction to a Suitably Stifling Stay-at-Home Thriller Reviewed online, Aug. 5, 2026. title: ‘The Last House’ Review: Greta Lee and Wagner Moura in a Claustrophobic Netflix Thriller Most Effective While the Threat Remains Unknown
full_text: × Skip to main content By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 11:59pm From left: Noah Alexander Sosnowski, Wagner Moura, Greta Lee and Riley Chung in 'The Last House.' Chris Baker/Netflix Flipping the home invasion thriller on its head, Netflix ’s The Last House puts a family in peril when a mysterious threat seals them inside their home with no escape while torrential rains pour down — for days that turn into weeks, months and years. Louis Leterrier ’s capable direction and reliably solid performances from Greta Lee and Wagner Moura as parents desperate to shield their kids from their worst fears make for a film that, despite its sci-fi and horror elements, is as much a psychological chamber drama and survival thriller about four people using their wits and dwindling resources to stay alive, even as their close-knit ties start fraying. Related Stories Movies Adam Sandler Celebrates 'Grown Ups 3' Starting Production: "We Missed You" Movies Louis Leterrier Says 'The Last House' Was the Hardest Movie of His Career -- and Explains Why He Can (and Can't) Wait for 'Fast 11' Inevitably recalling the isolation of COVID lockdown, the screenplay by Matthew Robinson ( Good Luck, Have Fun, Don’t Die ) oscillates between finding comfort and terrified vulnerability in self-reliance, keeping the exact nature of the force imprisoning the family — and seemingly everyone else in the world — vague until roughly an hour in, when the suspense is turned up even as the storytelling gets wobbly. The Last House The Bottom Line Lockdown redux. Release date : Friday, Aug. 7 Cast : Greta Lee, Wagner Moura, Riley Chung, Noah Alexander Sosnowski, Emma Ho, Gabriel Barbosa, Arden Cho Director : Louis Leterrier Screenplay : Matthew Robinson Rated PG-13, 1 hour 52 minutes That wait might frustrate genre fans requiring a more instantaneous stream of high-intensity thrills and scares, or anyone expecting the kind of hard-charging action Leterrier is best known for (the first two Transporter films, Clash of the Titans, Fast X and the forthcoming Fast Forever ), but the actors keep it watchable. The quote from Arthur C. Clarke that opens the film is significant: “How inappropriate to call this planet Earth when it is clearly Ocean.” With global sea levels rising due to climate change, those words could ultimately turn out to be prophetic. The pervasive anxiety attached to such environmental issues contributes to the tensions eating away at the family as they struggle to figure out who or what is holding them captive and what that entity wants from them. For much of its running time, The Last House feels almost like a more grounded version of the taut 2023 Kaitlyn Dever sci-fi horror No One Will Save You , this time rooted in human response to an ambiguous, possibly alien threat. Right from Day One, when they are grasping for answers, Jason Delgado (Moura) tells his family that whatever force has left them housebound is not man-made. But like the audience, he is making conclusions based on minimal concrete knowledge. An unemployed engineer, Jason packs up his fishing gear and heads home from the pier as a major storm front moves in, with no catch to show for his early morning efforts. A voiceover identified only at the end tells us: “The day the rains came, we learned we were not alone.” When Jason hustles his loving wife Ann (Lee), their 12-year-old son Graham (Noah Alexander Sosnowski) and 8-year-old daughter Ruth (Riley Chung) out to the car to go buy a Christmas tree, they find the doors and windows of the house sealed shut. Any attempt to force them open or even smash through them proves futile. Looking out their windows, the Delgados discover that their neighbors are in the same position, including a retired couple across the street who have limited food supplies. At first, Jason and Ann encourage the kids to stick to a routine — household chores, study, piano practice, PE time — convinced the rain will soon stop and their lives will return to normal. With the Wi-Fi out along with TV and radio reception, entertainment options are limited to board games, Jason’s old vinyl collection (a sweet moment has the family cutting a rug to The Cure) and a choice of two films, Annie or Air Force One , to throw into an old DVD player. They start rationing food, and Ann begins collecting tomato seeds and vegetable roots to start an indoor garden. One of the advantages of a house in disrepair and sinking into its foundations is easy access to soil by lifting a few floorboards. A crack in the chimney spurs Jason to rig a trap with which he goes “fishing,” catching squirrels and other wild animals that wander into the yard and end up in the frying pan. But this food source also brings a new danger into the house. Somehow, the need to hide from whatever is outside becomes imperative, even more so when they catch their first partial glimpse of a towering creature, unrecognizable as any species known to man. Their confinement stretches on, jumping ahead five years, by which time the orderly suburban street has surrendered to overgrown nature. The children grow into teenagers, Graham (Gabriel Barbosa) becoming moodier and more impatient while Ruth (Emma Ho) retreats into her vivid imagination, reading about mermaids and mythological monsters like Krakens and Leviathans. She starts theorizing about undiscovered sea creatures living on the ocean floor. Things get hairier once the tentacled entities outside reveal themselves and the family is forced to fight them off. But the creature designs are clunky, dipping for inspiration into H.P. Lovecraft, kaiju, the rampaging river mutation in The Host and a whole mishmash of unmemorable sci-fi freaks. The more we see of them and the more their presence is explained, the more the film slips out of Leterrier’s grasp, cheapened by tired jump-scare tropes like corpses bobbing up in water or bodies infested with creepy-crawlies. We’ve seen too many more terrifying depictions of families pitted against outsize nonhumanoid aggressors — in the world of A Quiet Place , for one — to be especially transfixed by the faceoffs here, which are less effective than the elemental menace of rising floodwaters threatening to drown the Delgados in their own home. After such a protracted emotional build-up, the conclusion feels rushed, its interspecies-empathy message a bit trite. The movie’s main strength is its emphasis on familial love as a sustaining force, nodding back to thrillers from the ‘80s. Ann and Jason might both appear to be cracking up under the strain, frightening their children — she becomes more fatalistic, while he is so consumed by his responsibility to keep them safe that he neglects his roles as husband and father — but the unbreakable bond holding them all together makes the stakes more real than Robinson’s script would indicate. Lee and Moura are gifted actors, especially compelling as the increasingly haggard Ann and Jason give up trying to mask their despair. And Graham and Ruth are superbly cast at both ages, creating an affecting portrait of family as a lifeline that keeps the audience in their corner even when the storytelling falters. title: Meta Owes $942M To New Mexico After Judge Rules In Social Media Case; Zuckerberg Promises Appeal
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Becomes Fastest Pic To Hit Half-Billion Mark At Domestic Box Office Read the full story By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Meta Owes $942M To New Mexico After Judge Rules In Social Media Case; Zuckerberg Promises Appeal Paramount’s Precipice: How David Ellison Could Salvage $111B WBD Merger (Hint – Call Kamala) It’s All About The Release Date: Diddy Gets More Prison Time After Dust-Up With Another Inmate View All August 6, 2026 10:42pm Mark Zuckerberg Getty In the second phase of New Mexico’s big bucks social media lawsuit against META , a judge today slapped the Mark Zuckerberg created tech giant with a penalty in the hundreds of millions of dollars and also put some potentially big restrictions about the company can and cannot do when it comes to kids being on their platforms. “Although Meta…social media platforms are a significant contributing factor to the current mental health crisis among New Mexico’s youth established by the substantial evidence in this case,” wrote Judge Bryan Biedscheid today ordering the company to payout $567 million to safeguard minors, hand over money to the state’s mental health treatment programs and put a hard limit of 90 hours a month on individual use of social media platforms. Related Stories News Meta Stock Tanks In Jittery Market On Massive AI Investment, Mixed Q2 News UK Government Unveils Plan For Midnight Social Media Curfew For Older Teens Still, in typical Zuckeberg fashion, almost immediately after Judge Biedscheid ordered Meta to pay to combat the consequences of Instagram and Facebook (WhatsApp got a pass), the company stridently denied there is a problem and vowed to take the whole thing back to court. Watch on Deadline “We disagree with the ruling and will appeal,” a Meta spokesperson told Deadline of the nearly $600 million that is now added to the $375 million the tech-giant was ordered in March to fork over to the Land of Enchantment. “We work hard to keep people safe on our platforms and have been transparent about the challenges of identifying and removing bad actors and harmful content. We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts.” BTW, the $375 million sum from the spring is based off the maximum penalty of $5,000 per violation for such mental health cases under New Mexico law. Now, in total, Meta is on paper paying out $942 million. While that sum won’t prevent Zuckerberg from being able to pay his Visa bill, it could have devastating growth potential for Meta when one considers the recent L.A. action and thousands of similar suits across the country. Put in context, Meta has a market capitalization of around $1.50 trillion. That’s a lot of dough, but not limitless — and state Attorneys General know it. Which is exactly the message New Mexico’s Raul Torrez was sending today. “This case has always been about protecting children, standing up for families, and making sure that one of the world’s largest technology companies cannot profit from practices that endanger young people without consequence,” Torrez said after the latest ruling was filed. “Today’s decision is a victory for every parent who has worried about what social media is doing to their child and every child who deserves to grow up safer online.” Q2 Revenue Surges With ‘Michael’; News On Sequel; CEO Backs Par-WBD Deal Sam Neill Filmed ‘Legend Of Zelda’ Role Before Death; Two Others Also In Cast Kit Connor Eyed For Cyclops Role In Disney/Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Pic WBD Q2 Stumbles On ‘Supergirl’; Fox Corp Surges Thanks To World Cup Ads Read More About: Comments

title: What Is It Like to Portray Nazi Heinrich Himmler? Martin Müller Shares His Experience on ‘I Is Another’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 6, 2026 10:00pm Martin Müller (left) and Claes Bang in 'I Is Another' Courtesy of Anke Neugebauer/Ostlicht Filmproduktion/Wega Filmproduktion Portraying one of the leading Nazis and architects of the Holocaust comes with all sorts of challenges, responsibilities and concerns for actors. Just ask Martin Müller, the German actor who plays SS leader Heinrich Himmler, known as the chief implementer of the Nazis’ so-called “Final Solution,” in writer-director Felix Randau ‘s I Is Another ( Ich Ist ein Anderer ), which world premieres on Friday, Aug. 7 in the Piazza Grande program of the 79 th edition of the Locarno Film Festival in Switzerland. Set in 1952, the film stars Claes Bang as Felix Kersten, the former massage therapist to Himmler, who gets ambushed by journalist Hedda ( Valerie Pachner ). Kersten claims to have helped thousands of concentration camp prisoners to freedom during the Nazi era by using his influence with Himmler, but Hedda has her doubts and wants to prove he is making himself look like a hero that he really isn’t. Related Stories Business How Many of This Century's Top 100 Films Have a "Nepo Baby Creative"? Your Guess Will Be Too Low News Minnie Driver Recovering After "Really Bad Car Accident" in France Casting the role of Himmler proved to be the production’s toughest challenge. “The only part that was really hard to cast was Himmler,” Randau tells THR . “I was looking for someone who could play a weasel kind of guy, but it was really, really tough.” He asked some actors about the role and got a less-than-enthusiastic reception. “They accused me of providing a stage for an evil guy like Himmler. I think that is really ridiculous and a big mistake because evil is a part of creation. If you ignore or neglect it, it will grow in the dark, and that’s what’s happening here in Germany, as we can all see.” That warning doesn’t come out of nowhere: the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has been on the rise in the country, becoming a far-right force to be reckoned with in an age of rising anti-immigration sentiment, economic worries and traditional party fatigue. In Germany’s 2025 federal election, the AfD came in second and has developed strongholds in the country’s Eastern states of the former GDR. Against that backdrop, Randau and his casting director, Suse Marquardt, cast their net far and wide, eventually landing on a talent best known for stage and TV work. “I’m really happy that we found Martin Müller,” Randau tells THR , lauding him for bringing to the role just what he was looking for and more. Martin Müller sits on a sofa next to director Felix Randau on the set of ‘I Is Another’ Müller joins an illustrious list of actors who have portrayed Himmler on screen. They include Stephen Graham , who played the Nazi in the war drama The Man With the Iron Heart (2017), Eddie Marsan , who featured as Himmler in the historical drama The Exception (2016), Matthias Freihof, who was Himmler in the Tom Cruise starrer Valkyrie (2008), Kenneth Tigar, who took on the role in the alternate-history series The Man in the High Castle (2016–2019), Ulrich Noethen, who portrayed Himmler in both the Academy Award-nominated Downfall (2004) and in My Führer – The Really Truest Truth About Adolf Hitler (2007), as well as Ian Holm, who stepped into the Nazi’s boots for the miniseries Holocaust (1978). For Müller, the role came through a longstanding connection with Marquardt. “I got an e-mail for an e-casting, and I did it with my coach and sent it to Suse, and she said, ‘the director wants to meet you’,” he recalls. “And Felix came to Munich, where I live, instead of me going to Berlin. We just met in a restaurant, and after two hours of talking, I asked him how many people he was meeting. And he said, ‘I’m fine with you. I just wanted to meet you.’ So I was very happy.” Landing the part came with its own reckoning, though, given the horrific things Himmler was responsible for. “It’s horrible to take on that role on the one hand, but on the other hand, it’s an interesting person,” Müller says. “He is a horrible person, but people who are a horror are always interesting for an actor. For this part, Himmler isn’t in action in concentration camps or anything like that. So, the film doesn’t show the real horror of Heinrich Himmler because it’s told via Felix Kersten. And he doesn’t tell us about all the horrors because he doesn’t want to be seen in a bad light.” Even so, some scenes were particularly hard to shoot, both emotionally and psychologically. “Claes and I had this scene where we had to discuss how many Jewish people we could save,” Müller shares. “We filmed this scene the whole night, and at the end, we said to each other that it was so disgusting to talk about numbers, like people were nothing. Himmler had no empathy and was really cold. In his mind, he was just organizing things. People talk about Heinrich Himmler as someone who saw himself as a mathematician of the Holocaust. For him, there were no human beings behind the numbers.” The role stayed with him well after filming wrapped. “It was really difficult to leave the character,” Müller recalls. “It was one thing to leave the four or five kilos that I had gained for the role behind. That was also very hard, and I just finished doing that. But the other thing was leaving this ugly character. These things just really stick with me. I just kept thinking, ‘what are politicians doing nowadays? Oh my God!’ For me, it’s a horror what the politicians are doing at the moment.” That physical transformation started with a simple request: “Felix asked me, ‘Could you be a bit more round in the face?’ So, I did less sport and ate more to gain four or five kilos.” As for research, Müller deliberately skipped studying other actors’ takes on the role. “I think he was a totally uninteresting person,” he says. “There aren’t any films or other [material] with private stuff about him. He was just hiding. With Hitler, Goebbels or Göring, we know a lot of private stuff. We have some speeches by Himmler, but we have no private recordings to know how he was talking when not giving a speech. So I just didn’t care about that but tried to do it my way. And keep in mind: It’s not the ‘true’ Heinrich Himmler in the film. It’s Heinrich Himmler as [told] by Kersten. And you don’t know what is true or wrong. That’s what the whole film is actually about.” THR

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Scores Biggest First Week in Box Office History
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 6, 2026 7:39pm Spider-Man and The Punisher (Jon Bernthal) in 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day.' Jay Maidment/Sony Pictures Logo text Spider-Man : Brand New Day is still catching new records as the Tom Holland -led movie continues its impressive start at the box office . Sony Pictures announced Thursday that director Destin Daniel Cretton ‘s film has landed the highest-grossing first week in domestic box office history. It has surpassed $500 million in North America in its first seven days, becoming the fastest film to reach that half-billion milestone by supplanting Avengers: Endgame , which hit the threshold in eight days after opening in April 2019. Spider-Man: Brand New Day has notched records at a head-spinning pace, which includes scoring the best-ever domestic box office sums for a Monday and a Tuesday . Brand New Day became the second-fastest feature to cross the billion-dollar mark globally when Sony announced Tuesday morning that it reached the threshold in six days, bested only by Endgame . Related Stories Movies 'Heartstopper' Star Kit Connor Eyed to Play Cyclops in Marvel's X-Men Reboot Movies 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Lands Biggest Tuesday in Box Office History Over the weekend, Brand New Day was in a neck-and-neck battle with Endgame for the biggest domestic opening weekend ever. On Monday morning, Sony confirmed that Spidey had indeed prevailed to claim the crown with $360 million , surpassing Endgame’ s $357.1 million domestic start, although the latter’s $1.2 billion global launch still held the record for its worldwide opening weekend. Spider-Man: Brand New Day also set records for the biggest Thursday previews and top Friday domestic sum , along with giving Sony its best-ever opening weekend. Hailing from producers Marvel Studios and Amy Pascal, it carries a $225 million production budget. Zendaya , Sadie Sink , Jacob Batalon, Jon Bernthal and Mark Ruffalo also star in the new movie from Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings filmmaker Cretton. It sees Marvel Comics’ signature hero enduring a lonely existence without his loved ones before an invisible enemy tracks him down. During a conversation with The Hollywood Reporter , Sony Pictures chief Tom Rothman noted that audience interest in stars Holland and Zendaya does not appear to be a passing trend. “They’re not popular because they’re popular,” the exec emphasized. “They’re popular because they’re talented, and they deserve their popularity. They’re lovely, decent, grounded, good-valued people, and they work really hard. So they’ve earned every ounce of their success.” Sony projects that Brand New Day will continue attracting audiences in the coming weeks as the summer starts winding down. Its second weekend will encounter fresh competition from such wide releases as One Night Only , Super Troopers 3 and Ice Cream Man . THR

title: Morgan Freeman Will “Overlook Some of the Glitches” in a Script If They “Pay You Enough”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Carly Thomas Plus Icon Carly Thomas Senior Editor, Digital carly_thomas_ Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 7:39pm Morgan Freeman Leon Bennett/Getty Images Even if a script isn’t that good, Morgan Freeman said he’ll still say yes if “they’re going to pay you enough.” During a recent interview with The New York Times , the legendary actor got candid about how he chooses the projects he wants to take on, especially six decades into his career . “If somebody offers you a job, it’s very nice if they’re offering you also an exciting script, but in reality, two or three things come into play,” Freeman shared. “What are they going to pay you? If they’re going to pay you enough, then you overlook some of the glitches in the script that happen to be there.” Related Stories Music Morgan Freeman Wants to Show You the Blues TV Zoe Saldaña and Nicole Kidman Are Back in the Fight With 'Lioness' Season 3 First Look “Sometimes you can mention things that are in the script that don’t quite work out for you and by and large, that gets worked out,” he added. Freeman already has a long list of accomplishments, most notably his Academy Award win for best supporting actor for Million Dollar Baby , in addition to four other Oscar nominations across his career. He’s also known for his roles in Invictus , The Dark Knight , Se7en and Driving Miss Daisy , among many others. But even at 89, Freeman has no plans of retiring from the industry or slowing down. “I’m like Clint Eastwood on that: Don’t let the old man in,” he said. “So, keep working. If you can get out of bed and don’t fall down when you do it, then you just count your blessings and keep moving. So, I’ll work as long as I can — as long as somebody says, ‘Do you want to do this part?'” As for whether he has any other dream roles that he has yet to take on, Freeman quipped, “No. I’m pushing 90 now. So, the roles that I wished I had been able to play, Denzel Washington will play.” Freeman most recently returned for Lioness season three, which premiered on Paramount+ earlier this week. THR

Three episodes in, Stuart Fails To Save the Universe has brought back seven actors from the original show in addition to the spinoff’s leading quartet of Stuart (Kevin Sussman), Brian Posehn (Bert), Lauren Lapkus (Denise) and John Ross Bowie (Kripke), and has killed off two OG characters in two different universes. First, it was Kunal Nayyar’s opening episode who was shot dead by Kripke . In Episode 3, it is Wil Wheaton , killed with magic by another Stuart Fails To Save the Universe lead character, Bert. Related Stories News 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & "Breaking Up" Beloved 'Big Bang Theory' Couple News 'Stuart Fails To Save The Universe' Stars On Stuart's Bold Move In Episode 2 As His Relationship With Denise Takes Off... What About Gary? Set in a world where magic is real and where, per the opening credits spoiler, “Bert is magic,” Wheaton is a representative of the Wizards Guild of America. He comes after Stuart for unwittingly enabling Bernadette (Melissa Rauch) to resume her demon form after she had been expelled from the guild and stripped of her magic powers. (You can read about Rauch’s return and Bernadette’s beef with the WGA here .) Bert shields Stuart from Wil’s deadly fireball, which leads to a magic fight to the death between the two that destroys most of the comic book shop and ends with Wil’s demise. (You can watch most of the scene below.) “I remember when the script was sent to me, and I was reading through it and not getting most of it because I hadn’t seen anything else,” Wheaton told Deadline. “We get to the magic shop, and I knew that I was going to be a wizard because I’d had a costume fitting, but I didn’t know anything about what it was going to be. What I see in the script is Wil Wheaton and Bert have an epic fireball fight, and I took a picture of it and I texted that picture to Bill and I just said ‘thank you.'” Wheaton spoke about the logistics of filming the fight, in which the Star Trek: The Next Generation alum also got to flash the Vulcan salute. “We had so much fun. Tom [Mahoney], the visual effects supervisor, and Brian and I really went through blocking and coordinating this entire fight sequence, and it was about like, well, how do you tease the fireball up in your hand, and how do you shape the fireballs in your hand?,” he said. “And for a particular kind of nerd, it’s a really big deal to be a wizard throwing a fireball, and to see that, like, I look so much cooler than I’ve ever looked ever in my entire life.” Wheaton revealed an Easter egg he had asked the show’s costume designer Valerie Klarich to incorporate into his costume — which she did. “The character that I play in Felicia Day’s series, The Guild , is Fawkes, he’s the leader of their rival guild. Felicia and I wrote a comic book together about him, and on the cover, there’s this really cool artwork that is Fawkes in a wizard’s robe with all these glowing runes on it. So Val said, ‘Do you have any requests for your costume?’ And I said, ‘If you could put some runes down the sides of the cloak, that would be really cool.’ And she said, ‘Yeah, we know a 3D printing guy who prints on fabric.’ So I got it.” He shared his reaction to the Fawkes-inspired cloak. “When I saw that, I was just like, there’s this great moment in Almost Famous where Lester Bangs says to the kid, ‘Oh no, they made you feel cool, and you’re not cool, so you’re trapped. They made me feel cool, and I’m not cool, and I was like, ‘This is an entirely fine place to be trapped.'” ‘Bert is magic” Posehn spoke of the cool and dark side of Episode 3 where Bert can do magic but he also is almost burnt at the stake for being a scientist. “People here think science is evil,” Kripke said about the magic-ruled alternate reality, to which Stuart responds in a rare topical comment on the show, “How is this different from our world?” “That was a funny episode, and then also that we play off it, where somebody goes, ‘In this world, science is forbidden,’ and Stuart goes, ‘Isn’t that kind of like our world?’ That joke I loved,” Posehn said. “But getting to be burned at a stake as a metalhead — it wasn’t a bucket list thing but getting to do it was super fun.” Posehn is known for his lifelong love for heavy metal which he has blended with stand-up comedy in his novelty comedy-metal tracks. There was another big draw for him in the episode. “I’m the biggest dog nerd you’re gonna meet, so having magic powers where I could make a puppy just transform out of nowhere — that was so fun to shoot,” he said. In the episode, Bert is asked by his acolytes to manifest life and he does it by conjuring up a puppy. “He was so excited about the dog, it was so cute,” Bowie said. “He was so, so pumped about the doggie they gave him.” Added Posehn, “Every time I had to be joyful when I said ‘Abracadabra puppy,’ it was like the easiest acting job I’d ever done because there was a puppy on my lap. So I’m like, ‘Hehehe, look at him! He’s adorable!’ That was super fun to play.” March of the Penguin In the episode, Bert also takes revenge on Kripke for not helping him when he was at the stake by turning him into a penguin sporting Kripke’s hair. Bowie spoke about the method acting involved in playing a penguin. “I went back to the the time in my life that I was a flightless waterfowl, and really went through a lot of sense memory on that,” he joked. “No, it was incredibly fun because I’ve never done mo-cap, I’ve never had one of those suits with the little buttons on them and the camera right in front of your face.” (L-R): Kevin Sussman, Brian Posehn and John Ross Bowie in Episode 3 of ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ There was some VFX wizardry involved in the transformation but also old-fashion practical special effects. “They built a mock-up of the comic book shop that was proportionally larger, and they put an elastic band around my knees so I had to waddle,” Bowie said. “It was really fun, and then the finished product looks amazing, and I love that he’s a penguin with my hair. I thought that was a really good choice to keep this magnificent coif on the penguin. Yeah, I enjoyed that a lot.” Q2 Revenue Surges With ‘Michael’; News On Sequel; CEO Backs Par-WBD Deal Sam Neill Filmed ‘Legend Of Zelda’ Role Before Death; Two Others Also In Cast Kit Connor Eyed For Cyclops Role In Disney/Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Pic WBD Q2 Stumbles On ‘Supergirl’; Fox Corp Surges Thanks To World Cup Ads More from this Story Arc Stuart Fails To Save The Universe August 6, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells” July 30, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & “Breaking Up” Beloved ‘Big Bang Theory’ Couple View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells”
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Becomes Fastest Pic To Hit Half-Billion Mark At Domestic Box Office Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Stuart Fails’ Creators On ‘Big Bang’ OG Return For WGA Strike Roast In Magic-Themed Episode 3 Where Wizards Seek “Residuals For Eternal Spells” ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death Prime Video’s ‘Ride Or Die’ To Be Submitted As Comedy With Stars Hannah Waddingham & Octavia Spencer In Lead Actress Consideration For TV Awards View All August 6, 2026 6:30pm Story Arc (L-R): Kripke (John Ross Bowie) and Stuart (Kevin Sussman) visit 'Big Bang's Bernadette in Episode 3 of 'Stuart Fails To Save the Universe' HBO Max SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episode 3 of HBO Max’s Stuart Fails To Save the Universe . Another episode of Stuart Fails To Save the Universe , another surprise — and dark — OG return. In Episode 3, it was Melissa Rauch reprising her role as Bernadette Rostenkowski. Like in Episode 2, where Penny, in an alternate universe, is with her former boyfriend Zack with no trace of her Big Bang husband Leonard, Bernadette does not have Howard’s last name and appears very much single. She is the focal point of a scene that skewers the 2023 WGA strike with “inside jokes that will be amusing to only 4,000 people in the world,” said Zak Penn , co-creator of the spinoff alongside Big Bang creators Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady . Related Stories News 'Stuart' Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Director Destin Daniel Cretton Talks Sadie Sink, That Ending & What Might Be Next The Episode 3 world is ruled by magic , so, to fix their broken alternate reality-hopping machine, Stuart (Kevin Sussman) and Kripke (John Ross Bowie) seek out Bernadette, a renowned local sorcerer. Turns out she is “all out of abracadabra.” What happened? “The Wizards Guild of America claimed I used my powers while we were on strike,” she explained. “What were you on stwike for?,” Kripke asked in his signature speech pattern where “r”s and “l” are replaced by “w”s. “Better dental, residuals for eternal spells. It’s ridiculous, we were out for six months, and basically everyone got a handful of magic beans,” Bernadette said. (You can watch the entire scene below.) For the uninitiated, the Wizards Guild of America shares the same moniker, WGA, with the Writers Guild of America, which Stuart Fails to Save the Universe creators are all members of. The 2023 WGA strike lasted five months with a minimum wage increase, viewership-based streaming residuals and AI protections among the gains in the new agreement with the studios. Melissa Rauch in Episode 3 of ‘Stuart Fails To Save the Universe’ Bernadette tells Stuart and Kripke that she was expelled from the guild for using her powers during the strike to bring her neighbor’s son’s adorable rescue dog Chocolate Chip back to life after he was hit by several cars. “I don’t see how that’s bweaking a stwike,” Kripke said. “Exactly,” Bernadette said, adding, “Let me tell you something about Wizards Guild of America. 90% of them don’t even work, and yet they get to vote.” While the percentage is not that high, non-working writers are the majority, representing more than 50% of the full WGA membership that gets to vote to authorize a strike and then to ratify a deal. That has been an ongoing gripe for some established writers and a cause of divide within the union. There was some difference of opinions among the Stuart Fails To Save the Universe creators too during a lively — and funny — interview with Deadline about the WGA strike jabs, which you can (and should) watch below. WGA members caught performing writing services during the strike get expelled, which happened again in 2023. Claiming that an appeal is not an option, Bernadette floats a reversal spell that would give her her powers back that requires “blood of an innocent,” which Stuart qualifies for and provides. Later in the episode, Big Bang ‘s Wil Wheaton shows up to reveal to Stuart that Bernadette is in fact a demon and is killed by Bert (Posehn) in a magic power duel. The episode ends with Bernadette, in a full-on demon form, terrorizing Pasadena and hunting for Stuart & Co. Lorre, Prady and Penn all participated in the 2023 strike and were on the picket lines. Penn has been the most active and public in his pro-WGA stance, having previously served on the WGA West Board of Directors and the union’s Negotiating Committee. (L-R): Bill Prady & Chuck Lorre during the 2023 WGA strike in front of a ‘Big Bang’ banner outside the Warner Bros. TV lot. DEADLINE: This seemed to me like I could hear Chuck’s voice, all the stuff about Wizards Guild of America. Chuck, you write that speech? And is this what you really think about this writers strike? LORRE : (laughing). PRADY : Oh, this is the Wizards Guild of America, an entirely different organization of wizards. LORRE : Of wizards, yes. The wizards are striking for all the good reasons, and strike breaking is… PRADY : It’s possible that section may include some inside jokes that will be amusing to only 4,000 people in the world. PENN : Also, we have different opinions on this issue, I’d like to say. There’s a continuum of opinions about those issues, but the joke, it can’t be pro-WGA and still be funny. Although let me point out, the WGA rep is right because she is a demon. PRADY : That’s right, Zak is right. The Wizards Guild of America is entirely correct in this episode. LORRE : She broke the strike by bringing Chocolate Chip back to life. PRADY : That’s a lie, that whole chocolate chip story is a lie. PENN : Yeah, she’s a demon. PRADY : She’s a demon. LORRE : Well, yes, but she was also using her powers, and she was supposed to not use her powers during the strike, right? PRADY : Well, we have a different understanding of the episode. I think that entire story is made up. LORRE : Oh, I don’t. PRADY : She makes up that story to get them to give her the blood. I think she made up the whole thing. PENN : You’re getting a little taste of the writers room. With her Demonic transformation, Rauch added a whole new shade of dark to Big Bang alums’ returns for the spinoff, following Kaley Cuoco’s ruthless Penny in Episode 2 and Kunal Nayyar’s deeply depressed Raj in Episode 1. The series’ creators spoke about Big Bang OGs relishing going dark in the spinoff. “Beyond,” Prady said. Added Lorre, “Beyond. It was fun to do something different, that was part of the promise, come and play with us, and we’ll make sure that you’re playing a version of your character you never got to play before, an entirely different approach to the character, and that was fun for the actors.” Q2 Revenue Surges With ‘Michael’; News On Sequel; CEO Backs Par-WBD Deal Sam Neill Filmed ‘Legend Of Zelda’ Role Before Death; Two Others Also In Cast Kit Connor Eyed For Cyclops Role In Disney/Marvel’s ‘X-Men’ Pic WBD Q2 Stumbles On ‘Supergirl’; Fox Corp Surges Thanks To World Cup Ads More from this Story Arc Stuart Fails To Save The Universe August 6, 2026 ‘Stuart’ Episode 3: Wil Wheaton, Brian Posehn & John Ross Bowie Talk Wizards, Puppies, Penguins, Fireball Fight, Easter Egg & That Shocking Death July 30, 2026 ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators On Episode 2 Surprise OG Star Return & “Breaking Up” Beloved ‘Big Bang Theory’ Couple View All Story Arc Read More About: Comments

title: Eli Roth Talks the Unrated Gamble of ‘Ice Cream Man’ and What He Hopes the Town Learns From ‘Obsession’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Brian Davids Plus Icon Brian Davids Writer PickYourBrian Follow Sign Up View All August 6, 2026 4:39pm Eli Roth promoting 'Ice Cream Man' during CinemaCon. Ethan Miller/Getty Images Logo text Last year, Eli Roth decided to take matters into his own hands. After his experience on Lionsgate’s $120 million video game adaptation, Borderlands (2024), went awry, the filmmaker launched his own soup-to-nuts company, The Horror Section , to bypass the studio system entirely. Together with his partners, Roth aims to shepherd genre films from development through release without forcing filmmakers to navigate layers of studio oversight and executive mandates that so often shape creative decisions. The Horror Section’s inaugural release is Roth’s unrated splatterfest known as Ice Cream Man , which opens wide through Iconic Events Releasing on Aug. 7. Throughout his career, Roth has had to pull some of his punches in response to MPA-driven studio notes and exhibitors’ longstanding preference to avoid anything that exceeds an R-rating. But one recent horror franchise shattered that convention, opening the floodgates for more unrated theatrical releases like Ice Cream Man . Related Stories Movies As Hollywood Frantically Searches for Next 'Obsession,' 'Backrooms,' TIFF's Midnight Madness Curator Has Vital Clues Movies 'Ice Cream Man' Review: Eli Roth's Small-Town Horror Flick Is for Diehard Slasher Fans, and Absolutely No One Else “There is a [theatrical] audience for the fully unhinged unrated movie with full-on gore,” Roth tells The Hollywood Reporter . “Once Terrifier 3 opened to around $20 million, all of a sudden, AMC, Regal, Cinemark and all the chains said, ‘Yeah, we will play an unrated movie.’” Following the success of his feature directorial debut, Cabin Fever (2002), Eli Roth enlisted his childhood friend Noah Belson to co-write a screenplay about a creepy ice cream man whose frozen treats transform children into bloodthirsty, maniacal killers. But its risqué premise in which kids brutally murder their parents and teachers made financing nearly impossible to secure, leaving the project to languish on a shelf for more than two decades. Roth ultimately dusted it off to kick-start The Horror Section, viewing it as the perfect calling card for the company’s slate of unapologetically offbeat genre films. Drawing inspiration from Steven Spielberg’s 24-minute Omaha Beach battle in Saving Private Ryan , Roth’s Ice Cream Man stages a 30-minute school-set sequence that unleashes nonstop mayhem involving roughly 100 child actors. Despite the set piece’s over-the-top bloodshed, the young cast and their parents joyously embraced the gory chaos. “The parents had to have visual eye contact with their children at all times, and they were coming up to me at the monitor. Mothers were like, ‘My daughter would love a fake head. Can you give my son a leg?’” Roth recalls mid-laugh. “Once we laid out the blood and guts, the kids just started playing tetherball with a head or jump-roping with guts. The parents came up to me after to say, ‘This is the most fun day my kid has ever had.’” After Curry Barker’s Obsession and Kane Parsons’ Backrooms combined to gross nearly $900 million at the global box office this past summer, Roth is weighing in on the two horror phenomenons. Obsession followed a path reminiscent of Roth’s own Cabin Fever , premiering at TIFF before igniting a bidding war and later becoming a highly profitable theatrical release. Roth believes the film should earn Barker and star Inde Navarrette the industry’s highest honors. He also reveals that he attempted to recruit Parsons and Backrooms after catching wind of the filmmaker’s viral YouTube series in 2022. “ Obsession should win best [original] screenplay, and Inde Navarrette should win best actress. Everyone else should be nominated because it’s that good,” Roth says. “Four years ago, I reached out to Kane Parsons about how much I loved Backrooms , but I think Peter Chernin [North Road] already had it then.” Roth cautions the town against hastily rushing to recruit more YouTubers in hopes of catching lightning in a bottle again. In his view, the success of both Barker and Parsons wasn’t simply the product of existing online followings. Each filmmaker was also surrounded by experienced producers and collaborators who served as mentors. Thus, Roth hopes the next YouTube creator to make the leap to features is afforded the same level of guidance and support. “We’ve had an incredible run [of YouTubers succeeding on the big screen], but I don’t necessarily think that YouTube is the answer. It’s a component. If you’re going to get someone off of YouTube, don’t just throw them into the system,” Roth says. “Pair these younger filmmakers with an experienced filmmaker like Jason Blum, Osgood Perkins, James Wan or the Duplass brothers so they can help bring out the best in their work. That will set them up for success like all the smart producers who surrounded Curry Barker and Kane Parsons.” Below, during a conversation with THR , Roth also discusses his personal note network on Ice Cream Man considering he no longer had to entertain studio notes. *** In the past, you’ve been beholden to studio notes because they were beholden to the MPA in order to get the movie into theaters with an R rating. But now you’re beholden to no one thanks to the Terrifier franchise’s introduction of unrated screenings? Well, beholden is probably the wrong word. The MPA adjusts with the tastes of the times, so I’ve had an amazing experience, and a really good open dialogue, with them. It was never a fight with the studios, but there were always disagreements that were impossible to prove. Someone would say, “Take this out. It’s going to offend audiences.” And I’d say, “No, when you go to see this movie, you want to be shocked and offended.” Sometimes, it’d be gore, and sometimes it’d be language. For Ice Cream Man , I didn’t want to have to deal with that. I wanted to make something that’s pure and raw and from my head. I wrote this movie with Noah Belson in 2003, and for years, people would read it and go, “You can’t do this. You can’t ask children to even perform these scenes. This is too insane.” And I’d say, “No, kids love gore. They love Halloween. I want to make this the craziest movie I’ve ever done.” Then I saw what Terrifier 3 did. There is an audience for the fully unhinged unrated movie with full-on gore, and the theater chains learned that people will come to see it in a theater. So once Terrifier 3 opened to around $20 million, all of a sudden, AMC, Regal, Cinemark and all the chains said, “Yeah, we will play an unrated movie.” Iconic Releasing and I went to CinemaCon, and I sat down with every theater chain. I said, “I’m starting this company called The Horror Section. If I make unrated movies, will you put them in your theaters?” And they said, “Absolutely. Anything you want to do, we can help tell the horror fans.” I also said, “You can get comedy on your phone. You can get drama on TV. But you can only get the true adrenaline rush of seeing a horror movie in the theaters. It’s like Coachella. You can watch a Coachella performance on your phone, but it’s not the same as being there. You can pirate a movie, but you cannot pirate the experience and adrenaline rush. All respect to streamers, but I’m not making horror movies for streamers. I am making horror movies that are theatrical events with the longest window possible.” And the theater chains said, “We will fully support you.” Then I put together the company, and I raised the money [a production budget of $5.5 million, plus a few million for P&A]. After 20 years, I know how to [make a movie]. I know how to write it, produce it, release it and publicize it. Now, between The Horror Section and Iconic, we have an incredible team, and we’ll see what happens when we put Ice Cream Man out on Aug. 7. Eli Roth on the set of Ice Cream Man . The Horror Section Now that you don’t have studio execs looking over your shoulder, who do you ask for notes on a draft or a cut? I’ve always gone to my writer-director friends. I’ve always been very thankful that I can go to Quentin Tarantino or Edgar Wright or Sam Levinson or Sean Baker or Ti West. If I had a cut of a movie that was ready before I showed it to the studio or released it, I’d go to different people that I really trust and know that they aren’t going to lie to me. They’re going to go, “Okay, this works, this doesn’t work.” Sometimes you want to save them till later in the process, but sometimes it’s earlier in the process. So there’s a group of filmmakers friends that I really trust to not lie to me and not let me fall on my face. This time, I went to Bob Murawski, one of the best editors; Michel Aller, who cut Thanksgiving ; and [Tarantino’s editor] Fred Raskin. They didn’t cut the movie; Matt Lyons did. But I trust Fred, Bob and Michel. They’re all friends. So I showed them the movie, and all three of them had such strong notes for me and my editor. I knew Bob would get it. He said, “This is Devil Times Five times 50.” Devil Times Five [aka People Toys ] is such an obscure pull. And then Quentin was like, “Yeah, Bob Murawski said it’s Devil Times 50 .” It’s a very specific language. Fred Raskin, who I’ve known since film school, is a friend. He watched it on a weekend and gave me really great notes. So I’ve always had a team of really, really smart filmmakers that I trust that will give me honest feedback. Charlie Storer as Piper in Ice Cream Man The Horror Section How did you shoot Ice Cream Man with 100 kids? And how did you get 100 kids’ parents to sign off on all the bloody mayhem? You cannot believe how many horror fans are out there. I was a camp counselor for three summers, so I love kids and love working with kids. When we were shooting the playground attack, I was super upfront because I knew people were going to Google my name. I was like, “We’re making a horror movie. I want this to be The Birds , but with kids going crazy and full-on gore.” So we were pretty clear about it, and anyone who didn’t want to be involved is generally not going to sign up. Once you put the kids in monster makeup, they get it. They love it. These kids have seen every episode of The Walking Dead . They may not have seen the Terrifier movies, but they have Art Crispies backpacks. Their parents were also younger than me, so they’ve watched my movies. The parents had to have visual eye contact with their children at all times, and they were coming up to me at the monitor. Mothers were like, “My daughter would love a fake head. Can you give my son a leg? My son wants an arm. My daughter needs more blood.” So they’re all huge horror fans. I made it a team exercise. I said, “I brought you here for a reason because I want everyone to have their moment. We’re all scene partners. We’re all going to make this great, but only if we all listen and work together. The more you listen to me, the more I’ll be able to put the camera on all of you.” It’s the same way I approached the riot scene in Thanksgiving . We had to break the kids every 45 minutes. By the time you bring them out and set them up and have the 20 stunt people get them in fake blood, you have one or two minutes to get the shot. It was the craziest day of shooting in my life. But once we laid out the blood and guts, the kids just started playing tetherball with a head or jump-roping with guts. They were all laughing, and the parents came up to me after to say, “This is the most fun day my kid has ever had. You were so sweet.” I’m very even tempered. I have good energy. I don’t yell. But they’re kids, and sometimes, you have to just roll with it. We were about to shoot a scene, and I was like, “Action.” Stunt people were hanging and ready to be pulled down, but no one was moving. There was a kid in the middle with his hand up, and I went, “Yes?” And he said, “My shoe’s untied.” And I said, “Okay, we’ll wait.” Then he put his hand up again, and I said, “Yes?” And he said, “But where’s my mommy?” And I realized he does not know how to tie his shoes because he’s too young. And I was like, “Can someone help him tie his shoes?” They generally also had no fear whatsoever, but when we lined up 100 kids to get the ice cream, we had one minute to get the shot. I started rolling the camera, and a bee came along. And one kid was like, “A bee!” Then they all ran, and that was it. So the bee was now directing my movie. But at the same time, they gave us moments that we could have never predicted. The energy they brought to the set was so wonderful. There were kids that were crying at the end of the shoot because they didn’t want to get out of the makeup. They were sad that it was over. It was this beautifully wild experience. They did arts and crafts with the brains. Overall, they know the difference [between reality and make-believe]. They know what pretend is. So it was a mix of Halloween and Christmas. You know what it’s like to have a low-budget indie horror movie premiere at TIFF to great fanfare before having a highly profitable theatrical run. So what lessons do you hope the town learns from the Obsession craze? Obsession should win best [original] screenplay, and Inde Navarrette should win best actress. Everyone else should be nominated because it’s that good. It’s just an incredible film. Everyone is realizing that there are YouTube creators who can bring their audience to the theater, which is amazing. If I was a teenager, I would’ve started on YouTube. But it’s not like Curry Barker was the biggest YouTuber. He brought in an audience, but the movie itself is what carried the word of mouth. Everyone was saying, “Have you seen Obsession ?” Four years ago, I reached out to Kane Parsons about how much I loved Backrooms , but I think Peter Chernin [North Road] already had it then. I remember going to a barbecue years ago, and all these nine-year-olds were talking about was Backrooms . So I went down a rabbit hole watching it all, and it was really scary. I thought, This kid [Parsons] is a genius . So Kane Parsons and Curry Barker have been at it for years, and they’re so talented. We’ve had an incredible run [of YouTubers succeeding on the big screen], but I don’t necessarily think that YouTube is the answer. It’s a component. If you’re going to get someone off of YouTube, don’t just throw them into the system. Pair these younger filmmakers with an experienced filmmaker like Jason Blum, Osgood Perkins, James Wan or the Duplass brothers so they can help bring out the best in their work. That will set them up for success like all the smart producers who surrounded Curry Barker and Kane Parsons. We want to raise that next generation for success. You don’t want a bunch of YouTubers to be given a shot and fall on their face to where people go, “No, that doesn’t work.” It’s about pairing them with veteran filmmakers so they can help grow their careers by making the best movies possible. *** Ice Cream Man opens in movie theaters nationwide on Aug 7. News ‘Stuart Fails To Save The Universe’ Creators & Stars On Premiere’s Shocking OG Death & Its Aftermath As Stuart Fails To Save the Universe revealed in the Episode 2 opening credits spoiler (You can read all about the show’s unique, ever-changing main title sequence here ), “Zack is in this one.” Zack, a recurring character on The Big Bang Theory played by Brian Thomas Smith, was Penny’s ( Kaley Cuoco ) dim-witted but kind-hearted on- and off- boyfriend while she and Leonard (Johnny Galecki) were broken up. Stuart Fails To Save the Universe , from The Big Bang Theory creators Chuck Lorre & Bill Prady and Zak Penn , has established a pattern with the first two episodes, each featuring a surprise return of a Big Bang Theory original cast member. Following Kunal Nayyar’s appearance as Raj in Episode 1 where he is shockingly killed by Kripke (John Ross Bowie), Cuoco showed up in the second episode alongside Zack (Smith).
